body:
Tested this PR as promised. Verdict: **the weld configuration now works, and works well.** I'd be happy to see this merged in place of my #120424.

**Setup**: built `0befbb3` and its merge-base `fd98f84` (Linux, dev_build). Weld = `angular_limit_enabled = true`, `angular_limit_lower = angular_limit_upper = 0`, `softness = 0`. Defaults unless noted.

**Synthetic harness** (40x20px boxes, mass 1):

| test | merge-base | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| welded pair, sustained torque 0.5s then release | drifts to ~180°, never recovers | 0.0° (pair rotates as one rigid unit) |
| 4-box cantilever off a static anchor, 10s under gravity | max 179°, 67px tip sag, visible jitter | max 4.4° transient, settles at 0.5°, <1px sag |
| 8-box welded chain dropped 200px onto floor, 6s settle | flat, 0.02° | 0.0° joint deviation |
| welded pair on floor, 5x mass-4 boxes dropped on top | 0.37° | 0.03° |
| overhung 12x-mass welded tip load, 10s | settles flipped (105° final, 178° max) | 0.27° final, no flip |

**Stiffness knobs** (mass-8 box dropped onto the tip of a 5-link welded cantilever):

| config | max transient flex | final error | load stays on tip? |
|---|---|---|---|
| defaults (60 Hz, bias 0) | 45° | 0.54° | no — springback flings it off |
| `Joint2D.bias = 0.9` | 50° | 0.02° | no |
| 120 Hz ticks | 24° | — | yes |
| bias 0.9 + 120 Hz | 23° | 0.2° | yes |

So the two knobs separate cleanly: per-joint `bias` governs steady-state rigidity (0.54° → 0.02°) but does not reduce the impact transient — the flex happens faster than any heal rate; physics tick rate is what shrinks the transient. Solver iterations (8 → 16) had no measurable effect on the weld. One caveat on the suggested contact bias 0.1–0.3: at 0.2, stacked heavy bodies visibly compress into each other and pop apart while settling; for stacking-heavy scenes the default 0.8 behaved better, and the weld held at ≤0.03° under either setting.

**Real game**: my brick-stacking party game has a power-up that welds bricks to whatever they touch (clusters of 2–5 pin joints, 180 Hz physics, bias 0.9). This scenario is why I wrote #120424 — on master, welded bricks visibly pivot and ratchet out of position. On this PR, a full play session with drift telemetry on every welded pair (2,625 samples): max anchor stretch 0.5px (97.6% at exactly 0), max angular drift 0.2°. No flips, no runaway, no jitter.

Remaining limitation, inherent to any iterative joint rather than to this PR: impulsive loads flex the weld for a few frames before the split-impulse correction heals it (a compound body would not flex at all). At 120+ Hz it's hardly noticeable in practice.

The synthetic harness is a small self-contained Godot project (one script, runs headless or windowed, prints the numbers above) — happy to share it here or PR it into godot-demo-projects/2d/physics_tests if useful.

*Disclosure: tests and comment were prepared with AI assistance (analysis, harness code, and drafting done interactively under my direction and review).*

Thanks for the comprehensive testing. I am glad it worked out. I would appreciate the test code if you could share it here.

I would particularly value any tests revealing the value of a high bias.

@Ughuuu  made some cool physics benchmarks for Godot, which has an interesting PinJoint2D test.

See videos of results below.


https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ebe88c07-49b7-45d3-892d-25ca38917690


https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/cdf72a4f-1ab4-40b3-b9cd-3d09bfedbdd2


In this [benchmarks-repo](https://github.com/Ughuuu/benchmarks-repo), Godot-Rapier (and I think Godot-Box2D) is set up with 4x sub stepping, which gives their joint solver an effective sample rate of 240fps (even while the physics rate is just 60fps). So for these tests I ran the Godot physics rate at 240fps (because I am trying to compare just the pinjoint equations). 

You can see that the old Godot pin joint still explodes, but this PR doesn't.

*This PR is doing better because of the split impulse bias pathway. Normally, this sort of large systemic test with bias based 'hard' constraints would not behave well. Adding 'softness' to the joint will allow the existing Godot Engine (and this PR) to not explode at 60fps, but it is obviously 'soft'.*

Here's the synthetic weld-test harness I used — **https://gist.github.com/Marenz/693d58f37c1237356e2128678a2a8a44** (single-script Godot project, runs headless or windowed). It tests the weld config (`angular_limit_enabled = true, lower = upper = 0, softness = 0`).

Run all tests:
```sh
godot --headless --path .
```
Individual test / stiffness knobs:
```sh
godot --path . -- --test=chainload --bias=0.9 --fps=120
```

Tests: `knock` (sustained-torque weld recovery), `cantilever` (4-box overhang under gravity), `chaindrop` (8-box welded chain dropped to floor), `stackload` (welded pair under falling mass-4 boxes), `chainload` (mass-8 box dropped on a 5-link welded cantilever — the high-bias case), `flip` (overhung 12x-mass tip load). Each prints a `RESULT` line with max transient, final error, sag, and joint deviation.

On this PR build the numbers reproduce what I posted above (e.g. `chainload` default: 45° transient / 0.54° final; `--bias=0.9`: 50°/0.02°; `--fps=120`: 24°; `--bias=0.9 --fps=120`: 23°/0.2°, weight stays on). Happy to fold it into `godot-demo-projects/2d/physics_tests` as a proper demo if useful.
